title: Wieland; or, The Transformation
description: A tale of religious fanaticism and mysterious voices in the Pennsylvania backcountry, and one of the first American novels to make psychological terror its subject. The book is narrated by a young woman who recounts the destruction of her family as a precarious narrative meant to instruct a listener. Its machinery of disembodied speech, inherited enthusiasm and suspected possession gave the American Gothic its first fully developed plot.
plot_or_argument: Clara Wieland recalls how her father, a German emigrant preacher, burned himself to death in his barn after mistaking his own zeal for a divine command. Years later her brother Theodore, raised in the same creed of feeling, is driven to murder his children and then himself by voices that seem to come from his father and from Clara herself. An itinerant pedlar named Carwin is discovered to possess an unusual power of duplicating voices without moving his lips, and the family friend who loves Clara suspects him of the trick. The novel closes with a search for Carwin in the city that leaves the deepest motive unexplained, so that reader and narrator alike must decide whether the agency was human or diabolical.
narrative_structure: Retrospective first-person narrative cast as a framed confession to a silent auditor; a second book introduces an independent narrator and shifts the investigation to the city, producing a deliberately uneven, two-part design.
principal_characters: Clara Wieland; Theodore Wieland; the elder Wieland; Carwin
literary_form: Gothic novel of terror in the self-described precarious-narrative mode, blending domestic romance, religious memoir and detective plot
historical_context: Written in the late 1790s in Philadelphia, a city then arguing over sectarian enthusiasm, Deism and the legacy of the Revolutionary rejection of authority. The novel transposes the British Godwinian enquiry into a dissenting sect led by a zealot father. Its anxiety about voices without bodies belongs to a decade of pamphlet wars about religious credulity and rational belief.
literary_significance: It founded the American Gothic by relocating terror from castles to sects, barns and wooden backcountry houses. Its treatment of enthusiasm as a disease of the imagination made it a source for later American fictions of interior voices. It is the earliest American novel routinely studied as a work of the first rank rather than as a curiosity.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed; the author announced the work in his own publishing imprint and defended it in a prefatory letter.
bibliographical_notes: First published at New York in 1798 in four volumes, printed for the author; the four-volume format and the prefatory letter on the precarious narrative are characteristic of the first edition.

title: Ormond; or, The Secret Witness
description: The second of the author's experimental tales and the most explicitly philosophical of them, built around a set argument about the power of character over conduct. A self-sufficient republican heroine is pursued by a misanthropic European sage who believes that human beings are the puppets of circumstance and of fascination. Its dialogue on liberty, dependence and female virtue makes it a novel of ideas as much as a tale of terror.
plot_or_argument: A young American woman of independent means and fixed principles forms an intimate friendship with a wealthy bachelor's sister and becomes the object of two very different suitors. One is a frank planter; the other is Ormond, a solitary thinker who denies the reality of virtue and resolves to prove that he can bend any will by art and fascination. He pursues her through disguise, surveillance and an appeal to her pity, and the crisis arrives when she must act without evidence on the character of the men around her. The ending leaves her security restored but the argument only partly answered, since Ormond's own conversion is reported at a distance.
narrative_structure: Third-person tale organized around a debate, with long set speeches and letters that interrupt the action; the secret witness of the title gives the plot its delayed revelations.
literary_form: Philosophical and moral tale in the Godwinian manner, inflected by Gothic suspense and by the domestic novel of conduct
historical_context: Published within a year of the author's first tale, during a brief American season of metaphysical fiction. The debate with which it engages was contemporary: whether a republic of equals could produce virtue without dependence, and whether female independence was defensible. Its European villain embodies Federalist anxieties about aristocratic artifice imported across the Atlantic.
literary_significance: It is the earliest American novel to make female self-sufficiency, rather than courtship, its central ethical problem. Its figure of the manipulating sage supplied a template for the American seducer-villain. It remains the clearest link between the Godwinian circle and the native Gothic.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published at New York and Philadelphia in 1799 in three volumes; it appeared without a London issue, unlike the author's first tale.

title: Arthur Mervyn; or, Memoirs of the Year 1793
description: A picaresque and documentary novel built around the yellow-fever epidemic that emptied Philadelphia in the summer of 1793. The first part follows an impressionable young draughtsman through the disease-ridden city; the second part pursues the thieves and shipboard villains who exploited the crisis. It is the first major American fiction to treat epidemic and commerce as historical forces.
plot_or_argument: An apprentice from a Pennsylvania village comes to Philadelphia and falls under the influence of a cultivated but amoral stranger who robs the sick and dying. As the fever turns the city into a place of flight, speculation and burial carts, the hero is himself exposed to contagion, quarantine and the collapse of the household that shelters him. An appendix of memoranda documents the mortality, the physicians' disputes and the benevolent committees with a historian's precision. Later the same villain resurfaces aboard ship and in the West Indies, and the hero's pursuit of him exposes the traffic in stolen goods and forged identities that the epidemic made possible.
narrative_structure: Two-part memoir by a first-person narrator, the first book closed by an inserted statistical and medical appendix; the second part continues the same voice in a wider geographic field.
principal_characters: Arthur Mervyn; Hawksfield
literary_form: Picaresque journey novel and city documentary; epidemic narrative with an embedded historical appendix
historical_context: The epidemic of 1793 struck the temporary national capital during the Jeffersonian contest over French and British allegiance, and its relief efforts were organized by voluntary committees. The novel draws on contemporary medical bulletins and on the public's argument about contagion and quarantine. Its second part reflects the anxious commerce of the 1790s Atlantic, including the slave trade and the flight of planters from Saint-Domingue.
literary_significance: It gave American fiction its first sustained treatment of an epidemic and of the city as an epidemiological space. The inserted memoranda anticipate the documentary realist mode. Its moral anatomy of profiteering in crisis has made it a persistent subject for histories of medicine and of the early republic.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed; the first part was issued serially and then collected.
bibliographical_notes: Part one published at Philadelphia in 1799; the complete two-part novel appeared in one volume in 1800, and the record takes 1799 as the beginning of publication.

title: Edgar Huntly; or, Memoirs of a Sleep-Walker
description: The author's most violently imaginative tale and the first American fiction to make the western forest a theatre of the unconscious. A sleep-walker pursues a murderer through the Pennsylvania wilderness and wakes to find himself the agent of the violence he thought he was investigating. It fuses the frontier captivity narrative with the German source-stories of somnambulism.
plot_or_argument: Edgar Huntly, living in a remote settlement with his friend Clitheroe, falls asleep while keeping a night-watch and, walking in his sleep, is attacked by a panther. Clitheroe, an English emigrant haunted by the accidental killing of a patron's son and by a love he believes he has forfeited, disappears into the woods after a night of somnambulism. Huntly follows him across the frontier, is captured by a party of Delaware warriors, escapes, and in a nocturnal trance kills sleeping men whom he takes for his enemies. The story ends with Clitheroe confessing from a prison cell, while Huntly's own responsibility for the deaths remains agonizingly unresolved.
narrative_structure: Epistolary memoir in three parts, addressed successively to a female friend and to the imprisoned confessor, so that testimony, dream and confession are all filtered through letters.
principal_characters: Edgar Huntly; Clitheroe
literary_form: Gothic sleep-walking tale and frontier captivity narrative in epistolary form
historical_context: Written on the edge of the Pennsylvania and Virginia frontiers where settler and Indian violence was a daily report in the newspapers. It borrows its medical framing from the new literature on somnambulism and dream. The political subtext concerns the displaced Delaware and the failure of treaty obligations in the trans-Allegheny west.
literary_significance: It is the founding text of the American wilderness as a figure for divided mind, anticipating later tales of sleepwalking, murder and pursuit. Its use of Indian capture reversed the older captivity formula by making the hero's own violence the real horror. It is central to the reputation of the American Gothic of the 1790s.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published at New York and Boston in 1799 in three volumes; its prefatory advertisement cites the genuine sleepwalking experiences that suggested the plot.

title: Salmagundi
alternative_titles: Salmagundi: A Miscellaneous Series
description: A series of miscellany numbers satirizing the manners, politics, literature and fashions of New York, issued in the Addissonian and Spectator tradition. The voices are those of a fictional club of idlers and observers, including a painter, a critic and a country wit. It created the American sketch-series and the persona of the detached, good-humored observer of civic life.
plot_or_argument: The numbers alternate between essay, character sketch, mock dissertation, song and reported anecdote, all directed at contemporary targets: the passion for improvements, duelling, pedantry, theatrical fashion, the antiquarian pretensions of local societies and the politics of the ruling party. A frame of club meetings and papers left behind by deceased members supplies the miscellaneous principle. The satire is personal rather than doctrinal, ridiculing the pretensions of the emerging literary and political class of New York.
narrative_structure: Serial periodical miscellany of twenty numbers, unified by a club frame and by recurring pseudonymous contributors rather than by plot.
literary_form: Periodical essay series in the Spectator and Independent Whig manner, with verse, character writing and burlesque dissertations
meter_and_prosody: Chiefly prose, with interspersed songs and occasional verse in common metres
historical_context: Published in New York between January 1807 and February 1808, in a season of fierce party conflict over embargo and the ruling family's New York allies. Its models were British: the Tatler, the Spectator, and the Anti-Jacobin review. The collaboration of three young writers, one of them still an apprentice lawyer, made the series the first American example of a literary enterprise organized on magazine lines.
literary_significance: It established the American sketch and character-series as a publishable form and introduced the urbane observer-persona that later defined the Knickerbocker school. Its parody of civic improvement set a permanent tone in American urban comedy. It is the earliest of the metropolitan periodicals that made New York a literary capital.
attribution_notes: Produced collaboratively by three New York writers; the batch records the series under its principal contributor, and the joint authorship was openly advertised in the numbers themselves.
bibliographical_notes: Issued in numbers at New York, 1807-1808, and gathered in volume form shortly afterwards; the individual numbers carry dates and a running series title.

title: A History of New York from the Beginning of the World to the End of the Dutch Dynasty
alternative_titles: A History of New York
Knickerbocker's History of New York
description: A mock-historical account of Manhattan under its Dutch governors, written in the invented voice of a deceased New England antiquary. It parodies annalistic history while inventing the colonial past as comic legend. The book supplied the etymology of Knickerbocker and the template for the American burlesque of origins.
plot_or_argument: The fictional historian begins with the creation and the discovery of the New World, then narrates the planting of New Amsterdam and the succession of Dutch directors in a style of inflated solemnity that turns every event into absurdity. A long digression on the arts of thinking and on the privileges of idlers sets out the book's burlesque philosophy of history. The reign of Peter Stuyvesant occupies the later books, with his quarrels, his wooden leg and his surrender of the province to the English. The history ends where legend begins, leaving the reader to decide whether the colonial past is a usable inheritance or a joke.
narrative_structure: Mock-annalistic history in nine books, framed by a publisher's advertisement, an essay on the historian and long ironic digressions; chronological narrative is constantly interrupted by disquisition.
principal_characters: Diedrich Knickerbocker; Peter Stuyvesant; the Dutch governors of New Amsterdam
literary_form: Burlesque pseudo-history and comic chronicle; mock-epic prose narrative with essays and digressions
meter_and_prosody: Prose, with interspersed verse quotations and songs
historical_context: Published anonymously in 1809 in the nick of a Federalist-Democratic-Republican quarrel in New York, and dedicated to a historical society in the manner of antiquarian works. Its jokes about Dutch inheritance answered the era's obsession with founding and lineage. The fabricated title-page, announcing the manuscript as the remains of a deceased antiquarian, was a knowing bibliographic fiction.
literary_significance: It created the founding myth of New York's Dutch past and gave the city the nickname Knickerbocker. Its method, comic scholarship in a ventriloquized voice, became the model for the American burlesque of history. It is the first American comic masterpiece to reach a British public.
attribution_notes: Published under a fictitious antiquarian author, Diedrich Knickerbocker, whose biography is invented in the front matter; the work is nonetheless unitary in composition.
bibliographical_notes: First published at New York in 1809 in octavo form, anonymously, with a title-page announcing the posthumous papers of the fictitious historian; reprinted several times with the author's name later disclosed.

title: The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent.
alternative_titles: The Sketch Book
description: A series of essays, sketches and legends by a persona who looks at England and at old New York with the same tender irony. It contains the two tales that became national property, a village schoolmaster and a sleeper who wakes a generation later, together with essays on Christmas, on the antiquities of the Inns of Court and on Westminster Abbey. The volume made the American sketch a transatlantic form.
plot_or_argument: The opening English papers, written in the voice of a retired essayist, meditate on lost friendships, on village churches and on the ceremony of old hospitality. The German and Dutch legends transpose European folk material into American settings: a sleepy hunter returns to find his world changed, and a nervous schoolmaster is undone by a headless horseman. Later English papers describe abbey, gallery and coach-roads as places where the past can still be felt. The concluding letters from an English visitor to his friends at home comment on theatre, society and the scenery of the British countryside.
narrative_structure: Loose miscellany of some three dozen papers under a unifying persona, with two internal sequences distinguished by setting: English essays and American or German legends.
principal_characters: Geoffrey Crayon; Rip Van Winkle; Ichabod Crane; Brom Bones; the headless horseman
literary_form: Sketch and character-tale series with familiar essays and legendary romance; the prose tale of the supernatural is folded into essayistic framing
meter_and_prosody: Prose, with a few verse addresses and songs in familiar stanzaic metres
historical_context: Written partly in England and published simultaneously in New York and London between 1819 and 1820, at a moment when American writers were still dependent on British publishing and British approval. Its English subject-matter answers the claim that the young nation had no picturesque past. Its Dutch-New-York legends were devised to give America an inherited legend of its own.
literary_significance: It established the literary sketch in America and made the short tale of willed belief a native form. Its two legends entered the schoolroom and the stage, becoming the most widely read American fiction before 1850. Its transatlantic double publication reshaped the terms of the exchange between American and British letters.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed; published under the persona rather than the author's own name, with the author identified in the advertisements.
bibliographical_notes: Published in seven paper parts at New York from 1819 and collected there in two volumes in 1820; a London edition in the same years was issued in weekly numbers.

title: Tales of a Traveller
alternative_titles: Tales of a Traveller, by Geoffrey Crayon, Gent.
description: A second miscellany of tales and essays, framed as the papers of a Travelling Bachelor and organized into three self-conscious divisions: German tales of the supernatural, sketches of Italy, and a burlesque third part on money and speculative schemes. It shows the sketch turning deliberately toward romance and satire. Its essay on the love of riches has been read as the first American meditation on speculation as a national pathology.
plot_or_argument: The German tales, translated from alleged source papers, give ghost, portrait and metamorphic stories in a schoolroom frame, including a bridegroom undone by an archbishop's curse and a painter whose portrait destroys his happiness. The Italian sketches pass from the Coliseum and the Catacombs to the robber stories of the Papal territory, where romance and banditry meet. The concluding division, a wallet of a late Travelling Bachelor, turns to the pursuit of money in a series of essays and projected schemes. Its unfinished shape, part legend and part satire, makes the book a laboratory for later romance.
narrative_structure: Three-part miscellany with an overarching persona; internal frames include a schoolmaster's translation of German manuscripts and the papers of a deceased bachelor.
principal_characters: Geoffrey Crayon; the Travelling Bachelor; the young editor and his schoolmaster
literary_form: Sketch series and supernatural romance in three parts, closing in essayistic satire on speculation
historical_context: Published in 1824, when its author was resident in Europe and the American market for metropolitan sketch-books was at its height. Its Italian material belongs to the post-Napoleonic tourist literature of the peninsula. The third part responds to the boom in banks, canals and paper schemes that prefigured the speculative manias of the 1830s.
literary_significance: It carried the German supernatural tale into American letters and supplied the model for the native ghost story of the 1830s and 1840s. Its essay on money is an early and searching critique of speculation as a national mood. Its unevenness is itself evidence of the sketch-book's limits as a form.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed; like the first miscellany it appears under the Crayon persona.
bibliographical_notes: First published at New York in 1824 in two volumes, with a London issue the same year.

title: The Alhambra
description: A sketch-book of the Moorish palace at Granada, part guide, part legend and part antiquarian romance, written after the author's residence in Spain. The ruins of the Alhambra supply both scenery and argument: a palace of the imagination that survives its own history. It closes the installment's American strand by turning the native sketch toward European decay.
plot_or_argument: A tourist sojourning in the monument recounts its Muslim history, its Christian occupants and its gradual degradation, then fills the courts and towers with legends of enchantment, treasure and lost beauty. Tales told by his Moslem guide and by the villagers about the palace alternate with essays on the tastes of travellers and on the value of Moorish ornament. The later numbers describe the search for hidden riches in the towers and the visitor's departure, leaving the palace as an emblem of transience.
narrative_structure: Miscellany of sketches, legends and antiquarian essays unified by the setting of the palace and by a travelling narrator's stay there.
literary_form: Local guide and topographical prose combined with romantic legend and the familiar essay
meter_and_prosody: Prose, with translated ballads and songs in stanzaic form
historical_context: Written after the author's stay at Granada in 1829 and published in 1832, in the season of the romantic recovery of Moorish Spain by British and American travellers and novelists. The monument was then a squatter's ruin as much as a museum. Its antiquarian romance belongs to the European vogue for ruins and for the expelled Islam of the peninsula.
literary_significance: It is the most durable American account of the Alhambra and fixed its legendary reputation for generations of travellers. Its mixture of guide-book and tale anticipated the later gift-book and keepsake miscellany. It completes the development of the American sketch into an archaeology of ruins.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published at London and New York in 1832 in two volumes; the English and American issues appeared in the same year.

title: The Precaution
description: A first novel in the fashionable domestic mode, set among American planters in England and America and concerned with pride, fortune and the marriage market. It imitates the contemporary English novel of manners and feels its way toward the author's later romance. Its argument about precautionary prudence in marriage is drawn from a sentimental ethics of self-government.
plot_or_argument: An American planter family resident in England is divided by a quarrel between two brothers over an estate and over the woman each loves. A proud father attempts to secure advantage for his children by arranging matches, while a disinherited younger son finds his own path in America. Misunderstandings about wills, fortune and rank are unravelled by disclosures late in the story. The precaution of the title, foreseeing and preventing the ruin caused by pride, is answered by marriage and reconciliation.
narrative_structure: Third-person domestic novel in the manner of contemporary fashion fiction, with letters and explanatory disclosures resolving the plot.
literary_form: Novel of manners and fashion; sentimental domestic fiction with a transatlantic setting
historical_context: Published anonymously in 1820, when American readers were still buying British three-decker fiction and native novelists generally began by imitating it. Its English setting reflects the post-war residence of American planters in the metropole. The decision to write it was encouraged by the recent success of a native historical romance.
literary_significance: It is the author's apprenticeship and the clearest American example of the Anglo-fashionable novel of the 1810s. Its failure as a copy and its interest as a document of cultural dependence are usually discussed together. It marks the starting point of the American romance of forest and sea.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously; the author disavowed and revised it in later collected editions, acknowledging its imitativeness.
bibliographical_notes: First published anonymously at New York in 1820 in three volumes; the author supplied a preface for the later American edition.

title: The Spy
alternative_titles: The Spy: A Tale of the Neutral Ground
description: The first important American historical novel and the book that created a native romance of the Revolution. Set in the neutral ground between the British lines and the American army in Westchester County, it makes espionage, disguise and neighbour-against-neighbour violence the substance of national history. Its pedlar of small wares, who turns out to be a spy of many identities, is the founding American figure of the disguised hero.
plot_or_argument: In the neutral ground of Westchester County, between the British lines in New York and the American army, the daughters of a Loyalist colonel are repeatedly thrown into the power of British officers, partisan leaders and the lawless skinners who infest the border. A pedlar of small wares, treated by both sides now as a simpleton and now as a knave, carries intelligence for the American command under a studied disguise. Hospitality, neutrality and betrayal alternate in a country where neighbour hunts neighbour, and where an old Whig widow's house becomes a refuge. The novel closes with the condemnation of a British officer taken as a spy and with the disclosure of the pedlar's real service to the American cause.
narrative_structure: Third-person historical novel with a choric neutral community at its centre; the plot of espionage is delayed by disguises and revealed at the close, in the manner of a discovered identity romance.
principal_characters: Harvey Birch the pedlar; Colonel Wharton; the Wharton sisters; Sarah the young Quaker; Kirkwood the deserter
literary_form: Historical novel and romance of the Revolutionary war, with picaresque disguise plot and topographical description
historical_context: Published in 1821-1822 from Westchester tradition, the author's childhood recollections and the histories of the war then current. It appeared in the same season as the Scottish historical romance and adapted its methods to republican material. Its treatment of Tory persecution reflects the nationalist reconciliation of the 1820s.
literary_significance: It gave American fiction its first historical romance and its first national hero of concealment. Its neutral ground became the model for the American frontier as a moral borderland. It made the historical novel the dominant American narrative form for a generation.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed; the author later added a preface and notes defending his use of documentary sources.
bibliographical_notes: First published at New York in 1821 in two volumes, with enlarged editions in 1822 and 1823 that added preface and historical notes.

title: The Pioneers
alternative_titles: The Pioneers; or, The Sources of the Susquehanna
description: The first of the series set in the New York backcountry and the earliest American novel to make settlement, law and the destruction of the forest its subject. A declining frontier county in the 1790s supplies a full social survey: judge, lawyer, doctor, Quaker, settler and Indian. Its portrait of an aging scout who prefers the wilderness to the courthouse remains the type of the American frontiersman.
plot_or_argument: In an outpost town on the sources of the Susquehanna, a family of landed English stock is joined by an heiress, and the neighbouring settlers contest game laws, land titles and the right to punish. An old huntsman, the finest woodsman in the county, is fined by the judge for shooting deer out of season and then dispossessed of his cabin by a legal technicality. A disguised prisoner turns out to be a son of the house, and an attempted marriage to a French count reveals the vulnerability of the heiress. The novel ends with the burning of the Indian winter village, the death of the Englishwoman and the huntsman's departure west to die.
narrative_structure: Third-person panoramic novel of a community, with a central action of legal dispossession and a subsidiary romance; the description of institutions repeatedly interrupts the plot.
principal_characters: Natty Bumppo; Judge Marmaduke Temple; Richard Jones; Elizabeth Temple; Oliver Edwards; Chingachgook
literary_form: Frontier romance and novel of settlement; social panorama in the manner of the Scottish historical novel
historical_context: Published in January 1823, drawing on the author's childhood in Cooperstown and on the land law, game law and Indian policy of the trans-Allegheny west. The year of its appearance saw the debate over the Indian removal bill, and the novel's dispossession plot answers that debate. Its topographical details were later supplied in a key by the author's family.
literary_significance: It created Natty Bumppo, the first permanently American heroic type, and made the conflict between wilderness and institution the masterplot of American fiction. Its legal and ecological conscience anticipated later environmental narrative. It is the foundation text of the American romance of forest and sea.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published at New York in 1823 in three volumes; the author's preface to the later edition discusses the fidelity of his frontier detail.

title: The Last of the Mohicans
alternative_titles: The Last of the Mohicans: A Narrative of 1757
description: The most widely read American romance of the colonial frontier, set during the French and Indian war in the Hudson Highlands and the wilderness west of Fort William Henry. Pursuit, capture and rescue give it a velocity unusual in the period. Its elegiac treatment of the extinction of the Mohican line makes the narrative of adventure also a narrative of dispossession.
plot_or_argument: Two daughters of a British colonel are conducted through the forest toward their father at Fort William Henry, escorted by a scout and his Mohican companions. An ambuscade by Hurons separates the party, and the sisters are carried off; one is rescued by an Indian runner whose claim to her is rejected, while the other is saved by the scout in a flight to a mountain fastness. After the massacre following the fort's surrender, the captives and fathers are reunited through a succession of escapes, a burning castle and a cave. The novel ends with the death of Cora in the flames, the killing of the Huron chief by the last Mohican, and the funeral of Uncas as the last of his people.
narrative_structure: Linear romance of pursuit and rescue in four-part alternation of scenes; a strong narratorial voice supplies topographical and ethnographic description between episodes.
principal_characters: Natty Bumppo; Uncas; Chingachgook; Magua; Cora; Alice; Heyward; David Gamut
literary_form: Historical romance and frontier adventure narrative, with elegiac frame
historical_context: Published in 1826 in four volumes, built on the campaigns of 1757 and on the author's own knowledge of the country around Lake George. Its appearance coincided with the national debate over Indian removal, and its theme of a people's extinction gave that debate a literary vocabulary. The novel's success was immediate on both sides of the Atlantic.
literary_significance: It defined the American frontier romance and established the Mohicans and the scout as the central figures of the national past. Its treatment of race, extinction and captive heroines remains the most contested aspect of the author's work. It is the best-known American novel of the 1820s.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published at New York and Philadelphia in 1826 in four volumes; reissued in the collected edition of 1827 and continuously thereafter.

title: The Prairie
description: The fourth of the frontier series and the first American novel to take the great plains west of the Missouri as its scene. The aged scout now lives among trapping parties and French settlers on the edge of the unexplored desert, and the plot turns on the chase of fugitives across a country without roads. Its philosophy of the wilderness as the last refuge of independence gives the book its seriousness.
plot_or_argument: A trapping encampment on the prairie is joined by an emigrant family and by a party pursuing two fugitives from the law, one of them an unprincipled man who has wronged his companions. The old scout acts as guide, judge and finally protector, and a midland settlement of French hunters and a hereditary chieftain of the Osage supply a social background to the chase. A fire on the plains, a secret cave used as a stronghold, and a duel before the tribe structure the later books. The novel ends with the death of the scout in the arms of his Mohican brother, the last of the forest men yielding the country to the prairie.
narrative_structure: Third-person romance in seven parts, with set-piece description of the plains and of the encampment; the pursuing party and the pursued alternate chapter by chapter.
principal_characters: Natty Bumppo; Chingachgook; Inez; the trappers and settlers of the encampment
literary_form: Frontier and maritime romance in the plains mode; philosophical tale of the state of nature
historical_context: Published in 1827, after the first federal surveys of the Louisiana Purchase had begun to make the plains imaginable to eastern readers. Its settlement politics answer the debates over public land and Indian title that led to the removal legislation of the following decade. Its topography was assembled from printed travels and from the author's own knowledge of the western country.
literary_significance: It moved the American romance from forest to prairie and made the empty continent a moral problem rather than a scenery. The death of the scout is the founding elegy of the American wilderness tradition. Its prophecy of a settled, commercial plains country is the series most influential passage.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published at Philadelphia in 1827 in two volumes, in a series of new tales, with simultaneous New York and London issues.

title: The Crater
description: The most speculative of the author's romances, a tale of a volcanic island in the Pacific on which a shipwrecked American sailor founds a theocracy. It joins maritime adventure to a political and religious analysis of a community built from scratch. Its second half, in which the island's priest-king degenerates into persecution, makes it a study of enthusiasm in a state of nature.
plot_or_argument: A New England seaman, passed over for his beloved's hand by a ship's captain, is cast away with a small company on an island newly risen from the sea. He marries the woman he loves, and the little community, cut off from all law, gradually accepts him as its religious leader. He founds a creed, a ritual and a chronology of his own invention, and his authority hardens into tyranny over those who doubt it. The narrative then carries a visiting ship and its passengers into the island's history, and closes with the overthrow of the priestly power and the return of the survivors to the world.
narrative_structure: Romance in two movements, the founding of an island community and its degeneration into persecution, framed by cosmological and geological disquisition.
principal_characters: Eric Berg; Martha Boardman; the shipwrecked company; the doubters of the island community
literary_form: Maritime and island romance with a philosophical argument about priestly power; utopian and anti-utopian fiction
historical_context: Published in 1827, in the decade of American South-Sealing voyages and of the published narratives that made the Pacific a theatre for moral experiments. Its theocratic plot belongs to the American argument about religious enthusiasm and republican government. The geological speculation reflects contemporary interest in volcanic theory.
literary_significance: It is the strangest and most ambitious of the author's fictions, anticipating later island narratives of conscience and domination. Its analysis of how a religious authority is manufactured from necessity has kept it in view for students of American theocracy. It shows the romance of forest and sea turning inward to political philosophy.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published at Philadelphia in 1827 in two volumes, as one of a series of new tales issued simultaneously in Philadelphia, New York and London.

title: Notions of the Americans, Picked Up by a Travelling Bachelor
alternative_titles: Notions of the Americans
description: A book of sketches and dissertations by a travelling bachelor who observes American politics, society, literature and manners with an irony often mistaken for approval. It is at once a defence and an indictment of the republic's institutions, directed as much against British prejudice as against American self-satisfaction. Its chapter on the conditions of a national literature is a founding document of American literary criticism.
plot_or_argument: The bachelor reports on elections, on the press, on banking and on the manners of the west and south, and on the diffusions of a commercial society. He then turns to the arts and to the question whether a country of equals can produce a literature, arguing that the American relation to English models is one of dependence rather than of inferiority. Its most discussed passages analyse the mechanics of party politics, and the notorious conclusion warns that the same public which destroys its dependencies will destroy its artists. The tone shifts from jest to prophecy without warning.
narrative_structure: Loose sequence of dissertations and reported observations under a single persona, framed by a preface that explains the licence of the travelling bachelor.
principal_characters: The travelling bachelor; the political and literary society of the United States as observed by him
literary_form: Familiar essay and character sketch combined with political dissertation; a book of national commentary
historical_context: Published in 1828, the year of Jackson's election, out of the author's residence in Europe and his renewed quarrel with British reviewers. Its politics were shaped by the Anti-Masonic and nullification agitation then beginning. Its argument about literary dependence repeats the terms of the periodical controversy over American letters carried on in Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine.
literary_significance: It is the most acute American analysis of the dangers of popular power before Tocqueville. Its account of the material conditions of authorship anticipated the sociology of the literary marketplace. It supplies the context for the romances of the same decade and for the author's later attacks on the American press.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published at Philadelphia and New York in 1828 in two volumes, with a London reprint in the same year.

title: The Bravo
description: A historical romance of republican Venice in the decay of its aristocratic power, and the author's most concentrated political novel. Its plot of a rescue from the council of ten exposes the machinery of a state that calls itself free. The book is unusually frank in treating a city as an idea, and its prefatory letter became a cause of controversy with the American press.
plot_or_argument: Two Venetian gentlemen, whose family has been ruined by the council of ten, seek to destroy the state and to free the Dalmatian islanders from Venetian rule. Their design is served by an adopted daughter who is loved by a boatman of the arsenal, and by a Greek captive whose loyalties are divided. The rescue of the conspirators from the prisons and the failed rising give the later books their momentum. The romance ends with the conspirators discovered, the boatman dead, and the republic's patience shown to be only another form of tyranny.
narrative_structure: Third-person historical romance with a tightly limited time and place; political expository dialogue between masked and unmasked citizens carries the argument.
principal_characters: Jacopo the bravo; the two young Venetians of a proscribed house; the Council of Ten; Venice
literary_form: Historical novel and political romance in the Italian setting; state-fiction of a declining republic
historical_context: Published in 1831, the year of the Italian risings and of the author's return from seven years in Europe. Its treatment of aristocratic Venice was read at home as an allegory of American party government. Its preface, discussing the conduct of the American press, provoked a prolonged newspaper war.
literary_significance: It completes the movement of the American romance of forest and sea into the political history of Europe. Its analysis of liberty as an institutional appearance influenced later American republicanism. It is the earliest American novel to treat the state itself as its main character.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published at New York and Philadelphia in 1831 in three volumes, with a London issue the same year; the preface on the press varies between the earliest numbers and the collected edition.

title: Thanatopsis
description: A meditation on death and the common receptacle of the earth, and the poem that announced the American nature lyric. Its argument is consolation without revelation: the dead are not lost but deposited in the same ground that holds all generations. The title, a view of death, names its method, and its blank verse gave American poetry its first authoritative meditative voice.
plot_or_argument: The poem opens by inviting the reader to attend to the voices of nature, which speak of mortality from the wood, the grove and the mountain. It then describes death as an inevitable and shared condition, in which every generation of humankind lies down in the earth together. The speaker consoles the mourner by making the grave a brotherhood rather than a solitary pit, and by describing the endless procession of the dead beneath the surface. The conclusion presents the earth as one great tomb in which the reader shall fall on and be at rest.
narrative_structure: Continuous lyric meditation in three movements, addressed to a generic reader and moving from observation of nature to the doctrine of the common grave and to consolation.
literary_form: Philosophical lyric meditation in the graveyard tradition, cast as a conversation poem addressed to nature
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse, iambic pentameter with irregular feminine endings and a suspended syntax
historical_context: First printed in a Boston review in 1811 in an imperfect text, and enlarged in the collected volume of 1821; the story of its publication by a parent without the young author's knowledge became part of its legend. Its stoical consolation belongs to the post-Calvinist religious climate of New England. The poem was read in Britain as evidence that American letters could rival the Lake poets.
literary_significance: It made the author the first American poet taken seriously in Britain and fixed the native meditative lyric on death and nature. Its blank verse set the standard for American philosophical poetry for fifty years. It remains the most anthologized American poem written before 1830.
attribution_notes: The circumstances of the first printing, and the share of the father's revision in the text, have been long debated; the authorship of the poem is not in doubt.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in The North American Review for January 1811 from a copy the author had not intended for publication; the authoritative text first appeared in the collected Poems of 1821.

title: To a Waterfowl
description: The shortest and best-known of the author's nature lyrics, in which a single bird flying across an evening sky becomes a lesson in providential guidance. The poem's argument is that the same power which directs the bird also orders the wanderer's steps. It is the central text of the American conversation with nature.
plot_or_argument: The speaker watches a waterfowl flying alone across the twilight, seeking its resting place on the marsh or the lake. He asks what guide directs the bird over pathless waters, and answers that no eye watches it in vain. The second movement draws the moral: the same power that teaches the bird his way will teach the poet, wandering alone, his path too. The poem closes with an act of trust, committing the wanderer's steps to that guidance.
narrative_structure: Two-stanza lyric of observation and application, the first stanza picturing the flight, the second drawing the consoling inference.
literary_form: Nature lyric and conversation poem addressed to a bird
meter_and_prosody: Alternating iambic tetrameter and trimeter in the common-metre hymn stanza, with regular rhyme
historical_context: Composed in 1811 on a solitary ride and long kept among the author's papers before appearing in print; the collected volume of 1821 gave it its permanent text. Its providential consolation belongs to the decline of Calvinist election in New England. The poem's currency in school recitation made it a national property by mid-century.
literary_significance: It is the model of the American lyric of single perception and moral inference, imitated for a generation. Its trust in a guidance revealed by nature rather than by scripture defines the author's religious imagination. It is the poem most often cited as the native counterpart of Wordsworth's shorter lyrics.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed; the date of the poem's first periodical appearance is reported differently in the biographical literature and is not asserted here.
bibliographical_notes: Composed in July 1811; the earliest text the batch can verify is that of the collected Poems of 1821, and the publication year is therefore left null rather than guessed.

title: The Embargo; or, Sketches of the Times
alternative_titles: The Embargo, or Sketches of the Times
description: A political satire in heroic couplets directed against the Jeffersonian embargo and against the administration that imposed it, written when the poet was a schoolboy. It is the earliest American poem of consequence to take national policy as its subject and to use the Augustan satiric manner for it. Its animus is Federalist, but its argument about the corruption of republican office looks forward to the author's later moral seriousness.
plot_or_argument: The poem denounces the laying up of ships and the ruin of commerce as the work of men who sacrifice their country's trade to a foreign policy of their own making. It attacks the venality of office-holders, the cowardice of the mercantile interest and the stupidity of a press that praises the measure. A second impression rewrote parts of the satire for a changed political moment. The closing invective promises that the embargo will be remembered as an example of how a free people may be misled.
narrative_structure: Continuous satiric argument in couplets, invective addressed to a party and to its measures, without narrative personages.
literary_form: Political satire and verse invective in the Augustan manner; occasional public poem
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets, iambic pentameter, closed and antithetical
historical_context: Written and printed in 1808, in the season of the Embargo Act, and reissued in revised form in 1809. Its politics are those of New England Federalism, and it was published at a time when a boy's authorship was itself a party argument. It belongs to the long pamphlet and verse war over the embargo and over non-intercourse.
literary_significance: It shows the transplantation of Augustan political verse into American party controversy and supplies the first documented instalment of the poet's career. Its couplet discipline marks the starting point of an American public poetry. It is the standard example of the juvenile political poem.
attribution_notes: Attribution established from the author's own later account of the broadside; the revised second issue differs materially from the first.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in 1808 as a separate poem, anonymously, the work of a schoolboy; a revised issue was printed for the author at Boston in 1809, catalogued as The embargo; or, Sketches of the times, and the two issues are often confused in the biographies.

title: Poems (Bryant)
description: The author's first collected volume, the book that made the American nature lyric a publishable career. It gathers the meditative blank-verse pieces, the shorter lyrics of natural observation and the juvenile political and classical verse. Its appearance with a British reprint in the same year marked the moment at which American poetry was accepted for import.
plot_or_argument: The volume collects the long meditation on death and the shorter lyrics addressed to a waterfowl, to a flower and to the fragments of the moralist's table. It includes translations and paraphrases from the classics and from Hebrew, a couplet satire, and the inscriptional verse written for a woodland walk. Its organizing principle is the alternation of large blank-verse meditation with small stanzaed observation. The effect is to present a single mind, retired from business, conversing with nature in the country it inhabits.
narrative_structure: Collected volume of separate poems arranged by length and form rather than by sequence; later enlarged editions reorganized the contents.
literary_form: Lyric and meditative collection; the first American volume of the nature lyric
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse for the longer meditations; iambic tetrameter and trimeter stanzas for the shorter lyrics; heroic couplets for the political pieces
historical_context: Published at New York in 1821 after the poems had circulated in review and newspaper, and reissued in London in the same year, a rare transatlantic honour. Its appearance coincided with the first confident claims for a national literature after the peace of 1815. The volume's blank verse made its claim on the authority of Wordsworth and of the British review tradition.
literary_significance: It established the American poetry of nature as an institution and gave the lyric meditation on death and the landscape its canonical form. Its reception in the British review shaped the transatlantic terms of the argument for a national literature. It remained the reference point for later American meditative verse.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published at New York in 1821 in one octavo volume, with a London reprint in the same year; enlarged editions followed in the 1830s, the last of these adding the prairie meditation.

title: The Prairies
description: The author's largest blank-verse meditation on the western grasslands, written in the season of the first American accounts of the prairie and printed just after the close of this installment's period. It contrasts the living hunting grounds of the plains with the vanished empires of Mexico and Peru. Its argument is that a wilderness people perishes with the coming of cultivation, and that the earth reclaims its own.
plot_or_argument: The poem opens on the boundless prairie and the herds of buffalo that people it, and on the Comanche hunter whose whole life is the chase. It then turns to the mounds of the west, the lost cities of Mexico and Peru, and the question of what becomes of races and nations when their country is taken from them. The earth is made the speaker's final authority, covering the works of men with grass and leaving the solitary hunter as a relic. The meditation closes with an act of submission to the destiny that removes one people to make room for another.
narrative_structure: Continuous descriptive and philosophical meditation in blank verse, organized by successive tableaux: the prairie, the chase, the mounds, the fallen empires, the earth's reclamation.
principal_characters: The Comanche hunter; the vanished mound-builders of the west
literary_form: Topographical and philosophical poem; the American extension of the descriptive meditation
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse, iambic pentameter with a sustained descriptive line
historical_context: Composed in 1832, when reports of the great plains and of Indian removal reached eastern readers together. Its imagery draws on the newly available travel narratives of the trans-Mississippi west. Its elegy for extinct races belongs to the public argument over the removal policy then being executed.
literary_significance: It is the author's most ambitious poem and the fullest American lyric treatment of the prairie as history and as moral problem. Its use of the mound-builders made a scholarly controversy into poetic material. It marks the transfer of the European descriptive poem into an American geography.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: Composed in 1832; the scholarly accounts consulted differ between 1832 and 1833 for its first periodical printing, with the poem added to the collected edition of 1834, so the publication year is left null rather than asserted.

title: A New-England Tale
alternative_titles: A New-England Tale; or, Sketches of New-England Character
description: The first novel by a New England woman to reach a wide American audience, and a direct attack on clerical bigotry and Calvinist discipline. It grew out of a religious tract and became a domestic tale of a girl rescued from an enthusiast's household. Its subject is the power of a hard teaching over a sensitive conscience.
plot_or_argument: A gentle and imaginative girl is thrown into the charge of a severe Calvinist minister and his household, where her scruples are tormented by a doctrine of election she cannot answer. She is protected by neighbours of liberal and rational religious opinion, and is finally delivered from spiritual tyranny by their countenance and by marriage. The tale interposes sketches of New England village life, of the free school and of the clergy as a class. Its argument is that a sect's discipline can damage a child's mind, and that toleration and education repair the injury.
narrative_structure: Third-person domestic novel with inserted tales and sketches; a didactic plot of spiritual oppression and deliverance framed by character portraits of clergy and neighbours.
literary_form: Sentimental and domestic novel; tract-derived tale of religious bigotry with sketches of manners
historical_context: Published anonymously in 1822, in the decade in which Unitarian and Calvinist parties in New England were contesting churches and colleges. Its author was the daughter of a Federalist congressman and had been converted under the influence of a Universalist preacher. The novel's satire of clerical authority is a document of the denominational quarrels of the 1820s.
literary_significance: It opened the tradition of the American domestic novel of religious persecution and of the woman writer's critique of the clergy. It established the model of the New England tale in which community and conscience are the real antagonists. It is an early example of fiction used as a party instrument in the Unitarian controversy.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously; attribution established from the author's own later acknowledgement and from contemporary correspondence about the tract from which the novel grew.
bibliographical_notes: First published anonymously at New York in 1822; the author's name was prefixed to later editions, which revise the religious satire.

title: Redwood
alternative_titles: Redwood: A Tale
description: A tale of an orphan girl brought from the wilds of the New Jersey forest into society, and the author's second novel. It combines the frontier story with the novel of sensibility and with an argument about inheritance and mistaken identity. Its forest scenes were among the first by a New England woman writer.
plot_or_argument: A young woman brought up in the seclusion of the New Jersey pine barrens is thought strange and proud by the settlement around her, and her ignorance of her own parentage is the source of the story's distress. Neighbours and incomers try in turn to explain her, and her exposure to the wider world of cultivation and kindred tests her temper and her principles. The recovery of the family history that gives her a place is delayed by disclosures withheld until the later books. Recognition and marriage close the tale, and the wilderness is left behind.
narrative_structure: Third-person novel of education and recognition, with a wilderness first section and a social second section; letters and disclosures carry the argument of inheritance.
literary_form: Sentimental and domestic novel; frontier tale of orphan discovery and recognition
historical_context: Published in 1824 in two volumes at New York and reprinted in London, part of the first wave of American fiction that found British publishers. Its New Jersey setting reflects the settlement and land disputes of the pine barrens. Its treatment of female independence continues the argument of the author's first novel.
literary_significance: It consolidated the position of the New England domestic novel of the 1820s and gave the woman-made frontier tale its earliest form. Its contrast between forest society and polite society is a genuine contribution to the wilderness theme. Its London reprint is evidence of the transatlantic market the author later helped to build.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed in later editions.
bibliographical_notes: First published at New York in 1824 in two volumes, with a London reprint in 1825.

title: Hope Leslie
description: The most ambitious early American historical novel by a woman, set in the Massachusetts Bay colony of the 1630s and 1640s. It makes the Pequot war, the treatment of Indians and the position of women in a theocratic commonwealth its joint subjects. Its famous argument is that the children of a Puritan generation may dissent from its creed and still be loyal.
plot_or_argument: Two sisters, one spirited and one gentle, are left in the care of a severe Puritan governor after their father is ruined by a quarrel with him. The younger elopes with a young Indian of the Pequot nation and passes out of the colony's world, while the elder is bound to an accomplished English youth whose loyalty to the settlement is tried by her obstinacy. The narrative passes to the Pequot war, to the burning of the fort at Mystic, and to the death of the sister whom the colony has lost. It closes by asking whether justice between cultures is possible in a country founded on conquest.
narrative_structure: Third-person historical romance alternating between domestic plot and public history, with a frame of chronicle and legend and a closing appendix of historical documents.
principal_characters: Hope Leslie; Faith Leslie; Everell Whittingham; Governor Winthrop
literary_form: Historical novel and romance of the colonial period, with domestic and frontier plotting
historical_context: Published in 1827, in the year of the removal debate, and written from the author's family recollections of New England colonial history. Its use of the Indian war answers the contemporary argument over the rights of the Cherokee and the conduct of the state. Its treatment of the cavalier and the roundhead inherits the Scottish historical romance.
literary_significance: It is the central fiction of the Puritan inheritance by a woman writer and one of the earliest American novels to make Indian dispossession its explicit moral subject. Its sister-plot supplies the structural model for later domestic historical fiction. It has been recovered as a canonical text of early American women's writing.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published at Boston and New York in 1827 in three volumes; the volume closes with an appendix of colonial documents.

title: The Backwoodsman
alternative_titles: The Backwoodsman: A Poem
description: A two-canto poem defending the western settler and the plain republican character against the pretensions of landed aristocracy and of borrowed European taste. It is one of the founding texts of Knickerbocker verse and an early statement of the claim to a national literature. Its argument is explicitly political, attacking the old Dutch family pride of the Hudson valley.
plot_or_argument: The first canto sets the backwoodsman's life against the luxury of the refined planter, and describes the log cabin, the clearing and the forest as the school of republican virtue. The second canto turns to the aristocratic pretensions of the eastern families and to the danger that borrowed European manners will corrupt a young country. The poem invokes the western emigrant as the true representative of the nation. It ends with an appeal to letters to be made on native material and by native conditions.
narrative_structure: Descriptive and didactic poem in two cantos, proceeding by contrast of settings and by invective against social pretension.
literary_form: Didactic and topographical poem in the eighteenth-century manner, with political argument
historical_context: Published at New York in 1818, when the western settlement and the old Hudson valley patroonships were live political questions. Its anti-aristocratic polemic belongs to the Democratic-Republican attack on the surviving families of the eastern elite. It appeared in the same season as the first native attempts to make a national poetry out of the forest.
literary_significance: It gave the backwoodsman a poetic dignity before the prose romance did so, and it is a document of the Knickerbocker group's formation. Its polemic against cultural dependence states the terms of the transatlantic argument of the 1820s. It helped to establish the western theme in American verse.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed; the author was later identified with a second, collaboratively written series.
bibliographical_notes: First published at New York in 1818 in a small octavo, with a second edition in 1819.

title: The Dutchman's Fireside
description: A tale of the old Dutch settlement on the Hudson, and the most durable of the author's fictions. Its spirited young heroine of the settlement is courted by two very different men, a quiet hunter of the woods and an idle schemer who lives on the neighbourhood's hospitality. The tale is a comic study of industry against idleness and belongs to the Knickerbocker recovery of the Dutch colonial past.
plot_or_argument: An attractive and managing young widow or maid of the settlement is courted by a quiet hunter of the woods and by a scheming idler who lives on the neighbourhood's hospitality. The idler's pretensions, his projects and his imposition on the family are exposed by degrees, while the hunter's worth is proved by service and by knowledge of the country. The tale moves between the fireside of the Dutch household and the woods and hills around it. It ends with the exposure of the idler and the marriage of the heroine to the hunter.
narrative_structure: Third-person comic tale of a settlement, with the domestic fireside as its centre and a chase and exposure plot at its edge.
literary_form: The sketch and character tale in narrative form; pastoral comedy of the old Dutch country
historical_context: Published in 1831, in the last phase of the Knickerbocker interest in the Hudson valley Dutch past and on the edge of this installment's period. Its quarrel between industry and idleness addresses the moral economy of a farming country under pressure from speculation. The date is given by the electronic census of early American fiction; some handbooks place the tale earlier, and the discrepancy is recorded rather than resolved.
literary_significance: It is the best of the Knickerbocker Dutch tales and an important source for the domestic representation of the Hudson valley. Its use of the idler as a social type belongs to the American comic tradition that the sketch series founded. It shows the frontier theme turned to the settled country rather than to the wilderness.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed; the first edition names the author as the writer of a prior poem.
bibliographical_notes: First published in the early 1830s, generally dated 1831, at New York; reprinted several times in the collected editions of the 1840s.

title: Alnwick Castle, with Other Poems
description: The first collected volume of the Knickerbocker poet of the group, containing the title meditation on the English baronial castle and the shorter pieces that had made his reputation in the newspapers. Its lyrics celebrate friendship, the ruins of the old world and the Grecian cause. The volume established the author as the poet of the New York literary group.
plot_or_argument: The long title poem visits the castle on the English border and draws from its state rooms and its ruins a meditation on the transience of feudal power and on the surviving dignity of the mind. The shorter poems include tributes to a dead friend, patriotic pieces and the lyric of the hunter's death, with versified recollections of the American scenery. The volume as a whole argues that a young country may inherit the picturesque through sympathy. Its closing pieces turn from European ruin to native promise.
narrative_structure: Collected volume organized by length and occasion, with a dominant topographical meditation and a group of occasional and elegiac lyrics.
literary_form: Romantic meditation and lyric collection; topographical verse with elegy and occasional poem
meter_and_prosody: Chiefly blank verse in the longer poem; iambic stanzas of varying length in the lyrics
historical_context: Published at New York in 1827, in the decade when the Knickerbocker group was defining itself against Boston and against British review criticism. The author's friendship with a fellow poet who died young gave the elegies their public currency. Its English subject answers the American claim that only Europe possessed ruins worth poetry.
literary_significance: It is the volume by which the Knickerbocker group possessed a poet, and its elegies on early death became a staple of the annuals. Its treatment of the castle ruin brought the European picturesque fully into American verse. It fixed the author's reputation, which stood high through the century and fell afterwards.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published at New York in 1827 by the firm of G. and C. Carvill in a small octavo; enlarged and collected editions followed from the 1830s.

title: Poems (Sigourney)
alternative_titles: Poems; by the Author of Moral Pieces in Prose and Verse
description: The first collected volume by the Hartford poet, issued without her name, and the book that made her the most widely read woman poet in America before the war. Its pieces take the occasions of mourning, the domestic round and the moral reflection of a Calvinist-minded but emotionally liberal piety. The volume established the native feminine verse of the annual and the gift-book.
plot_or_argument: The poems move through elegy on the dead, meditation on bereavement and the consolations of nature, moral reflections on female duties and on the trials of life, and descriptive pieces on American and Italian scenery. Several poems address the deaths of children and of friends, and others treat poverty, old age and the obligations of the survivor. The volume's argument is that feeling rightly disciplined is a form of knowledge. Its closing pieces turn from private mourning to public and religious duty.
narrative_structure: Collected volume arranged by class of subject, with elegy, meditation and descriptive poem as the organizing forms; no narrative sequence.
literary_form: Lyric and elegiac collection in the sentimental and meditative tradition; occasional and devotional verse
meter_and_prosody: Iambic stanzas of common and church metre, with longer meditative passages in pentameter
historical_context: Published at Boston and Hartford in 1827, and issued anonymously in a season when women's authorship was commonly disguised. Its success was secured by the review press and by the new monthlies and annuals that needed poetry. Its religious manner belongs to the post-Calvinist piety of Connecticut and western Massachusetts.
literary_significance: It founded the American tradition of feminine occasional and elegiac verse, and its poems became the standard copy for the mourning and gift-book market. It shows the economics of anonymous women's publishing at the moment of its success. Its range of moral and domestic topics defines the feminine voice in American letters before 1850.
attribution_notes: Issued anonymously; the author's identity was established within a few years and her name was prefixed to later editions, which were enlarged and reorganized.
bibliographical_notes: First published anonymously at Boston and Hartford in 1827, the title-page naming the writer only as the author of an earlier prose and verse volume; several enlarged editions followed.

title: The Genius of Oblivion and Other Original Poems
description: A volume of occasional and meditative verse by a widowed mother of five children, published with the help of her late husband's lodge and the author's first book. Its longest poem personifies oblivion as the power that veils the past and finally releases the mourner. The book marks the beginning of the most influential editorial career in American letters.
plot_or_argument: The title poem addresses oblivion as the gentle power that draws a veil over the sorrows and the errors of the past, and asks whether remembrance is a blessing or a burden. Shorter pieces treat death, bereavement, the seasons, the duties of the survivor and the prospects of the republic. Several poems take public occasions and national subjects, and others are elegies on private losses. The volume's movement is from grief toward resignation and then toward useful labour.
narrative_structure: Collected volume with one dominant personification poem and a company of shorter occasional pieces; no imposed sequence.
literary_form: Lyric and meditative collection; personification poem, elegy and occasional verse in the sentimental manner
meter_and_prosody: Iambic pentameter stanzas and heroic couplets, with hymn-like shorter metres
historical_context: Published in 1823 after the death of the author's husband left her without means, and supported by subscription and lodge patronage. Its appearance belongs to the first great decade of women's periodical and gift-book writing in America. Its national poems answer the post-1815 demand for a republican verse.
literary_significance: It is the first monument of a woman of letters who would dictate the taste of American households for half a century. Its treatment of oblivion and remembrance shows the psychology of sentimental verse turned to the service of bereavement. It documents the patronage economy by which women's books were first financed.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously; the authorship was established by her own later account and by the subscription records of the first edition.
bibliographical_notes: First published anonymously in 1823 with the financial help of the lodge of her deceased husband; the volume's later fate was overshadowed by her editorial career.

title: Mary's Lamb
alternative_titles: Mary Had a Little Lamb
description: A short lyric narrative for children about a lamb that follows its keeper to school, and the most memorized American poem of the nineteenth century. Its stanzas treat the animal's fidelity as a lesson in affection and in the proprieties of the schoolroom. It became the standard specimen of the juvenile verse of the common school.
plot_or_argument: A little girl owns a lamb that follows her wherever she goes and waits at the school door. Its appearance in the schoolroom provokes laughter and study among the pupils, and the teacher's attempt to exclude it fails. The lamb's constancy is made the poem's moral, and the child's attachment its feeling. The poem closes on the picture of the animal waiting, faithful and patient, after the lesson is over.
narrative_structure: Narrative lyric in several quatrains, progressing from statement of the fact to the schoolroom incident and to the closing image of fidelity.
principal_characters: Mary; the lamb; the schoolmaster and the pupils
literary_form: Juvenile lyric narrative in the common-school manner; songlike stanzaic poem
meter_and_prosody: Alternating iambic tetrameter and trimeter quatrains with simple rhyme
historical_context: Printed in 1830, in the season of the new juvenile magazines and the common-school readers that created a national market for children's verse. Its subject, a child and an animal, is the characteristic material of the juvenile annual. It was set to music and carried into the schoolroom by the readers and by the author's own periodical work.
literary_significance: It is the best-known American poem for children before the war and a permanent item of the national memory. Its transmission shows how a poem of occasional authorship becomes folk property. It is the standard example of the sentimental juvenile lyric.
attribution_notes: Attribution long established, though the poem's currency in song and reader has encouraged legend about its origin; the incident is generally reported as domestic rather than invented.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1830; the account of its inclusion in the author's juvenile collection cannot be dated confidently from the sources consulted, and that volume's date is therefore not asserted here.

title: Logan
description: The first in a rapid series of American romances by the era's most combative critic, and an early and violent treatment of the Indian question as a grievance rather than a picturesque. It locates its story in the Susquehannah valley and in the border warfare of the western settlements. The book announces its author's programme of an unrivalled and undecorous native style.
plot_or_argument: A tale of the western valleys in which an Indian war and the ruin of a household are bound together by a single provocation. The narrative dwells on the injustice that converts a people's patience into revenge, and on the fate of those caught between the settlement and the forest. Its characters speak in a bold, compressed style that refuses the decorum of the ordinary frontier tale. The action ends in death and retribution rather than in reconciliation.
narrative_structure: Third-person border narrative of great compression, with long rhetorical passages and abrupt shifts between settlement and forest scenes.
literary_form: Frontier and Indian tragedy in prose; the border tale treated as a moral and political indictment
historical_context: Published at Philadelphia in 1822, the earliest of the author's native romances and the first of a rapid series. Its treatment of Indian grievance belongs to the last years before the removal crisis of 1830. The book appeared while its author was still identified with Baltimore journalism rather than with the settled literary establishment.
literary_significance: It is the boldest of the pre-removal Indian novels and the first American attempt to write border tragedy as indictment. Its style, abrupt and rhetorical, was the provocation its author later theorized in his criticism. It anchors the argument for the originality of American frontier fiction before the genre settled into a single dominant hand.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed; the standard dating of the first edition is 1822, though some handbook accounts give 1823.
bibliographical_notes: First published at Philadelphia in 1822, from the press of H. C. Carey and I. Lea, with the title-page locating the tale in the valley of the Susquehannah.

title: Seventy-Six
description: A novel of the year of the Declaration of Independence, and one of the earliest American attempts to write the Revolution as popular comedy rather than as civic legend. Its scene is a New England town and its personages a company of ordinary men swept into the war. The book treats patriotism as a matter of temperament and of incident.
plot_or_argument: In a community on the eve of the war, neighbours are divided by interest, habit and fear as the crisis arrives, and the call to arms draws each of them into the contest by a different motive. The narrative follows the enlistments, the quarrels and the comic misadventures of a company raised from the town. Private interest and public duty are played against one another until the war settles the argument. The book ends with the Revolution established and the community transformed by the demands made on it.
narrative_structure: Third-person popular novel of a community in crisis, episodic and crowded with speech-types, with the historical year imposed as frame and title.
literary_form: Historical novel of the Revolutionary period in the comic and popular manner
historical_context: Published at New York in 1823, in the efflorescence of centennial and semi-centennial interest in the founding events. Its plebeian treatment of patriotism belongs to the author's quarrel with the dignified historical novel. The book was written when its author was editing a newspaper and preparing his move to English publishing.
literary_significance: It is among the first American fictions to make the Revolution available as popular comedy, and it anticipates the later native treatment of the founding as everyday history. Its crowded speech and provincial idiom are an early experiment in American vernacular. It documents the range of the historical novel in the 1820s.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published at New York in 1823; the edition consulted for this record gives no reliable information about volume count, and that detail is omitted.

title: American Writers
alternative_titles: American Writers: A Series of Papers
description: A series of critical papers surveying the literature of the United States for a Scottish monthly, and the earliest attempt to write the whole of American writing as a single history. It reviews the colonial poets, the pre-war dramatists, the novelists and the critics with an energy that is as often abusive as judicious. Its polemic against cultural dependence is the most concentrated statement of American literary nationalism of the 1820s.
