plot_or_argument: The papers take up the writers of the colonies and of the early republic in turn, from the Puritan sermons and the verse of the eighteenth century to the native novelists and critics then living. Each account is used to argue that American letters have been misjudged by British condescension and underserved by American caution. The series demands a literature of national character, produced by native conditions and judged by native standards. Its closing papers turn the argument against the timidity of the American writer himself.
narrative_structure: Serial critical survey in a succession of magazine numbers, organized by author and period rather than by theme, with a running polemical argument.
literary_form: Critical review and periodical essay; the first history of American literature in serial form
historical_context: Contributed to Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine from December 1824 into 1825, at the centre of the transatlantic quarrel over American books conducted in British monthlies. Its author was then the American correspondent of the Scottish magazine and a pioneer of the professional review-writer. The series was written between his novels and helped to make the phrase American literature current.
literary_significance: It is the founding document of American literary history and of the claim that a national literature exists as a subject for criticism. Its quarrel with Edinburgh and London defines the terms of transatlantic cultural dependence for a generation. It established the review essay as an instrument of literary nationalism.
attribution_notes: Attribution established from the author's own later claims and from the magazine's records; the series was published in the periodical's customary manner.
bibliographical_notes: Published in Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine in a run of numbers beginning in December 1824 and continuing through 1825; no separate first edition appeared within the period.

title: Brother Jonathan
description: A historical novel of the Revolutionary war and of the Connecticut Yankee, published in Edinburgh at the height of its author's engagement with British romantic fiction. It takes the popular figure of the shrewd New Englander and puts him in the machinery of war, intrigue and border adventure. The book is an early study of provincial character as national character.
plot_or_argument: Through the campaigns and privations of the war, a company of New Englanders and their British and Loyalist antagonists are drawn into a succession of surprises, disguises and escapes. The Yankee of the title turns his homely craft to the business of intelligence and survival, and the narrative treats his shrewdness at once as comedy and as a national capacity. Private feuds and family claims run under the public history until the war resolves them. The tale ends with the peace established and its characters changed by what the contest made them.
narrative_structure: Third-person historical romance in three volumes, episodic and heavily dependent on reported speech, interweaving military history with private intrigue.
literary_form: Historical novel of the Revolutionary period; provincial comedy in romantic machinery
historical_context: Published in 1825 by the Edinburgh house that also issued the author's criticism, in the decade when British publishers took charge of American reputations. Its use of the Yankee type answers the English interest in American character after the war of 1812. The book belongs to the same burst of historical fiction as the author's other native romances.
literary_significance: It is the most elaborate of the antebellum novels to build a nation's character out of a provincial type. Its treatment of the Yankee as a form of knowledge anticipates later American comic realism. It documents the dependence of the American historical novel on Edinburgh.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published at Edinburgh in 1825 in three volumes, with a simultaneous American issue; the volume count is reported in the bibliographical accounts consulted.

title: Rachel Dyer
alternative_titles: Rachel Dyer: A North American Story
description: The most notorious of the author's early romances and the one he defended as a declaration of literary independence in a prefatory manifesto. It is a Gothic tale of colonial North America, moving between the province, the sea and the Indian country. Its style of violent compression and its refusal of moral decorum made it a scandal and a landmark.
plot_or_argument: A young woman of the province is bound by affection and by circumstance to men whose loyalties are divided between settlement, sea and war, and the narrative pursues her through capture, disguise and catastrophe. The colonial Indian war supplies the machinery of pursuit and reprisal by which the characters are tested. A tale of the ocean runs alongside the provincial story, giving the book its sense of a continent in motion. The action closes in death and in exposure of the hypocrisy that caused it.
narrative_structure: Third-person Gothic romance with alternating provincial, maritime and Indian-war lines of action, introduced by an ironical unpublished preface that states the author's programme.
literary_form: American Gothic tale and historical romance of the colonial period
historical_context: Published at Portland, Maine, in 1828, in the season of the removal debate and of the American Gothic's return after its 1790s vogue. Its prefatory manifesto answers the British review criticism with which its author had been engaged for four years. The book is the earliest of the American romances to treat colonial war as Gothic matter.
literary_significance: It is the central text of the author's programme of literary independence and the boldest American Gothic of the 1820s. Its theory of style, delivered in its prefatory argument, anticipated later American experimental prose. Its treatment of colonial violence gives it a place in the history of the Indian romance.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published at Portland in 1828 by Shirley and Hyde, in two volumes, with the prefatory account of the work's design much discussed in the critical literature.

title: Tamerlane and Other Poems
description: A slim first pamphlet of romantic verse, issued in Boston without the author's name and now one of the rarest books in American literature. Its title poem is a long confession of a wanderer who has forfeited love by ambition, and the accompanying pieces treat loss and solitude in the manner of the younger romantic poetry. The volume is the starting point of the author's career and of his lifelong quarrel with the hack writers.
plot_or_argument: In the title poem a solitary wanderer recalls a love withdrawn from him and a destiny of exile that he has chosen for himself, and he recounts a life of conquest abandoned for remorse. The shorter poems dwell on bereavement, on the memory of the dead and on the consolation or the emptiness of the natural world. The volume's movement is from the expansive romance of the long poem to the compressed elegy. Its speaker is a creature of will and of guilt rather than of observation.
narrative_structure: Pamphlet collection: one long narrative-confessional poem followed by shorter lyrics and an address to a patron of the imagination.
principal_characters: The wanderer of the title poem; the lost beloved
literary_form: Romantic narrative poem and lyric collection in the Byronic manner; confession in verse
meter_and_prosody: Iambic pentameter and mixed stanzas, with a dominant blank-verse recitative
historical_context: Published in Boston in 1827 while its author was a student in the city, in a small run of which very few copies survive. Its manner imitates the available romantic models, and its appearance preceded by two years the metropolitan review war over American letters. It belongs to the first generation of American poets writing after the British romantic example had become unavoidable.
literary_significance: It is the rarest and most quoted of American poetry pamphlets and the document from which the author's career is dated. Its Byronic confession supplies the native origin of the poetry of guilt and exile. It is the starting point of the American strand's closing phase in this installment.
attribution_notes: Issued anonymously, the title-page naming only the city of the author; attribution rests on the author's later acknowledgement and on the bibliographical census of the pamphlet.
bibliographical_notes: First published at Boston in 1827 in a small octavo of about two dozen pages, the author described on the title-page only as a resident of that city; surviving copies are extremely few.

title: Al Aaraaf, Tamerlane, and Minor Poems
alternative_titles: Al Aaraaf, Tamerlane and Minor Poems
description: The author's second pamphlet of verse and his first attempt at a cosmological poem. Its central fancy is an island or star of the same name, the residence of souls too imperfect for heaven and too delicately raised for earth. The volume reprints the earlier Tamerlane confession and adds short lyrics, and it shows the romantic habit of the sublime pushed to the verge of abstraction.
plot_or_argument: The title poem places the reader in a kingdom of the sky where the spirits of the imperfect dead await their final elevation, and describes its lakes, its night flowers and its waiting inhabitants. The poem then descends to earth and to the love and ambition that could not be satisfied there, and closes with a prophecy of the soul's eventual passage. Tamerlane supplies the second long poem, the wanderer's confession of forfeited love. The minor pieces treat the memory of the dead and the power of beauty to detain the mind.
narrative_structure: Two long poems followed by shorter lyrics; the principal poem proceeds by description of an imagined place, then by reflection, then by prophetic conclusion.
principal_characters: The spirits of the island of Al Aaraaf; the wanderer of Tamerlane; the lost beloved
literary_form: Romantic philosophical poem and lyric collection; vision-poem of the intermediate state
meter_and_prosody: Iambic pentameter with irregular stanzaic grouping, and shorter lyric stanzas in the minor poems
historical_context: Printed in 1829 for the author, after his expulsion from West Point and during his brief association with the family that had supported him. Its astronomical fancy borrows from the popular astronomy and from the German romantic example then reaching American readers. The volume sold poorly and was disowned by its author in later years.
literary_significance: It contains the earliest American poem to make a cosmology the scene of moral instruction, and it documents the ambitious, unreadable side of the author's imagination. Its revision history shows the author reshaping his early verse into a canon. It is the middle term between the 1827 pamphlet and the collected volume of 1831.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed; the volume names its author on the title-page.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1829, printed at Baltimore and offered for sale also at New York, in a small octavo; the title-page form of the title omits the comma before and, which the batch records as an alternative title.

title: Poems (Poe)
alternative_titles: Poems, Second Edition
description: The author's first collected volume of poetry and the most contentious of his early books, printed while he was a cadet at West Point. It gathers the two long poems, revises them heavily, and adds the shorter lyrics that became his permanent repertoire. Its prefatory prose letter denounces the current state of American poetry with a boldness that cost him readers.
plot_or_argument: The volume reprints Tamerlane and Al Aaraaf in shortened and recast form, the latter reduced from a two-part cosmological poem to its descriptive core. It then presents the shorter lyrics: an address to a classical beauty, a lament for the dead, a song of the valley of unrest, a hymn of the intellect and a meditation on a doomed city. The prefatory letter argues that American verse is made by imitators who flatter their public, and that the true critic must be willing to be hated. The book as a whole is a claim to professional standing rather than a miscellany.
narrative_structure: Collected volume with a prose letter at the head, followed by two revised long poems and a group of shorter lyrics arranged without a stated principle.
literary_form: Lyric and romance-in-verse collection; the first American example of a poet's self-canonization by revision
meter_and_prosody: Iambic pentameter and mixed lyric stanzas, with a marked experiment in long-line melody
historical_context: Published at New York in 1831 and subscribed for by a small circle, while its author was an artillery cadet; the volume's attack on living reviewers provoked a newspaper response. It belongs to the period in which American poets were negotiating the terms of a professional literary career. Its revision of the earlier poems reflects the working practice of a writer who reissued his verse throughout his life.
literary_significance: It fixes the author's poetic canon in its first public form and shows his method of revision at work from the outset. Its prefatory letter is an early American statement of the doctrine of the critic against the public. The volume is the source of the lyrics, including the address to Helen and the city of the sinking towers, that later critics treated as his characteristic mode.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed; the volume designates itself a second edition, counting the two earlier pamphlets.
bibliographical_notes: First published at New York in 1831 in a small octavo designated second edition; the text of Al Aaraaf is materially abridged from that of 1829.

title: To Helen
description: A short lyric of classical beauty addressed to a woman whose loveliness is figured as a ship arriving from a warm sea into a harbour of the soul. It is the poem that made beauty, and not desire, the author's enduring subject. Its three stanzas move from simile to arrival to a scene of the beloved as a torch-bearer of the antique world.
plot_or_argument: The beloved's beauty is compared to the barks that, wind-laid upon a perfumed sea, bear weary wayfarers to their native country. The poem then asks what the tired wanderer would give to reach the casements of that shore and the Niche where the Faun stands, half-embowered in the fragrant lilies of the stream. In the last stanza the beloved comes across the night with shining feet, and the region of the poem is disclosed as a home to which the wanderer belongs.
narrative_structure: Three-stanza lyric, each stanza developing one figure: the arriving ship, the shore and its shrine, the beloved's approach by night.
principal_characters: Helen; the weary wayfarer
literary_form: Romantic lyric of idealized beauty; address-poem in the Horatian and classical manner
meter_and_prosody: Iambic trimeter and tetrameter stanzas of nine lines with an intricate rhyme scheme
historical_context: First printed in the collected volume of 1831, where it stands among the poems the author's later editors classed with his verse of youth. Its classical furniture belongs to the schoolroom Hellenism of American colleges in the 1820s. The lyric was revised and reissued through the following decade.
literary_significance: It is the earliest of the author's lyrics to enter the permanent anthologies and the source of his reputation for the poetry of beauty. Its treatment of the beloved as a vessel of homecoming set a pattern for later American lyric addresses. It marks the moment at which his verse left cosmological ambition for the short perfect form.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed; the title under which the poem is known was settled in the author's lifetime.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in the New York volume of 1831; the text was revised in later collected editions, and the batch records the poem by its conventional title.

title: The Doomed City
alternative_titles: The City in the Sea
description: A vision of a dead city sinking in a strange western sea, published in the collected volume of 1831 under this title and reissued later as The City of Sin and as The City in the Sea. Its image of a town of towers mirrored in still water, watched over by personified Death, is the author's most durable tableau. The record keeps the title the poem actually bore within this installment's period.
plot_or_argument: The poem describes a city of amber towers lying level on a silent sea in a strange western country, where no wind blows and no wave stirs. The towers, the domes and the palaces are reflected in the water, which is a dim mirror of the abyss. Death, as an entity, sits robed and crowned above the town, and the scene is presented as the lake of unmannerly and unquiet things. The closing movement suggests that the waters will at last rise and swallow the city in one consummation.
narrative_structure: Continuous descriptive vision in two movements, the tableau of the city and the presence of Death, ending in a prophecy of dissolution.
principal_characters: Personified Death; the doomed city and its towers
literary_form: Romantic vision poem and descriptive meditation; the tableau poem of terror
meter_and_prosody: Iambic tetrameter and trimeter stanzas with long reverberant vowels and repeated refrains
historical_context: Printed in the 1831 collected volume as a separate poem, at a moment when the author was building his theory of the unity of poetical effect. Its imagery belongs to the repertory of the European picturesque and of the graveyard meditation, transferred to an oceanic scene. The poem's later titles track its repeated revision through the 1830s and 1840s.
literary_significance: It is the source of one of the most often reproduced images in American verse and a laboratory for the author's later doctrine of the single effect. Its revisions across three titles make it a case study in his practice of recasting. It closes the American lyric strand of this installment at the point where the vision poem and the short effect-poem meet.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed; the three titles denote successive stages of one poem rather than separate works, and the batch keeps the earliest.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in the New York volume of 1831 as The Doomed City; it reappeared as The City of Sin in 1836 and in its final form as The City in the Sea in 1845, outside this installment's period.

title: The Life of Washington
alternative_titles: The Life of Washington, with Curious Anecdotes, Equally Honourable to Himself, and Exemplary to His Young Countrymen
description: A biography of Washington written for the young by an itinerant book agent and preaching minister, and the most widely circulated American life of the first president. It established the pattern of the exemplary national life built on anecdote and on the reader's feelings. The cherry-tree story of German honesty, added in a later edition, became the founding fable of American juvenile biography.
plot_or_argument: The narrative follows Washington from the anecdotes of his childhood through the surveying and the French-and-Indian war to the command of the Continental army and the presidency. Each stage is illustrated by short stories of honesty, temperance, courage and courtesy, offered as models for imitation. The book dwells on the death at Mount Vernon and on the national mourning, and it urges the young reader to make private virtue the ground of public service. Its final pages bind the character of the man to the character of the republic he left behind.
narrative_structure: Chronical biography broken into anecdotal episodes, with moral reflection addressed directly to the juvenile reader; the appendix of maxims and sayings grows with each edition.
principal_characters: George Washington; his mother; the planter and surveyor of the northern neck; the slaves and household of Mount Vernon
literary_form: Prose biography for juvenile instruction; exemplary life with anecdotic and moral apparatus
historical_context: Published within a year of the death of Washington in 1799, when the national mourning created an immediate market for his life. Its author was a Methodist preacher turned book canvasser who sold subscriptions in the southern and western country. The expansion of the text through the editions of the 1800s answers the new American demand for a usable founding mythology.
literary_significance: It is the most influential single book in the American culture of character, and the origin of the anecdote tradition in national biography. Its invention of a private Washington for the classroom defined how generations learned the founding. It is the canonical example of the juvenile and educational book of the early republic.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed; the additions that make the book famous belong to later issues rather than to the first text.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1800 in a small octavo compiled for the entertainment and instruction of young people; it passed through many editions and enlargements in the author's lifetime, the well-known cherry-tree anecdote appearing in an edition of the second decade of the century whose number and year are variously reported.

title: Modern Chivalry
alternative_titles: Modern Chivalry: Containing the Adventures of Captain John Farrago, and Teague O'Regan, His Servant
description: A picaresque comic novel of the western Pennsylvania republic, published in parts across more than twenty years, and the earliest American fiction to make popular politics and office-seeking its sustained subject. Its captain and his Irish servant travel a country of elections, militias, speculators and sectarians. The book is a satire on the pretensions of a society that has abolished ranks but invented new ones.
plot_or_argument: Captain John Farrago, a half-learned frontier lawyer, sets out with his servant Teague O'Regan, an illiterate Irish adventurer, through the settlements and camps of the western districts. Teague, emboldened by flattery, aspires to every office in turn, from legislator to bishop, and each ambition ends in exposure and humiliation. The narrative interposes the captain's long discourses on chivalry, law, religion and government, and a company of Germans, Quakers, Methodists and speculators. The novel closes with the follies punished and the captain wiser than his servant.
narrative_structure: Episodic picaresque in a succession of separately published volumes, with discursive chapters, embedded tales and a running argument between master and servant.
principal_characters: Captain John Farrago; Teague O'Regan; the candidates and office-seekers of the western districts
literary_form: Picaresque and journey novel; comic satire of the republic, in the fielding manner
meter_and_prosody: Prose, with interspersed verse and song
historical_context: The first volumes appeared in 1792, with further volumes in the following decade and the completed work issued in its final form in 1815. Its scene is the western Pennsylvania of the Whiskey excise troubles, land speculation and rapid settlement. The author was a Princeton graduate, a teacher and a judge of the western circuits, and the book's politics are those of a skeptical republican lawyer.
literary_significance: It is the first major American comic novel and the earliest native analysis of popular office-seeking as a social comedy. Its western setting makes it a founding text of the frontier tradition in prose. Its long publication history is a document of the instability of the early American literary marketplace.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed; the novel was published in parts, and the several volumes carry different title-page dating.
bibliographical_notes: Begun at Philadelphia in 1792 with the first two volumes, continued in the 1790s and completed in its last form in 1815; the first edition is the bibliographer's standard case of a novel assembled over two decades.

title: Greenfield Hill
alternative_titles: Greenfield Hill: A Poem, in Seven Parts
description: A topographical, historical and didactic poem on a hill settlement in New Haven county, and the most ambitious verse of the early American republic before the 1820s. Its seven parts pass from the scene of the grove to the history of the country, its institutions, its commerce, its religion and its morals. It gives the American township as a subject for the Thomsonian and Goldsmithian descriptive manner.
plot_or_argument: The poem opens on the grove and the vale of Greenfield Hill and its seasons, and then retells the settlement of the country from the first planting of the colony. It passes to the survey of the neighbouring towns, to the character of the people, to the pleasures of study and to the claims of religion and of public duty. Admonitions against intemperance, gambling and irreligion are woven through the descriptive passages. The close commends the hill, its church and its schools to the reader as a model of a republican community.
narrative_structure: Descriptive and didactic poem in seven parts, moving from local scene to colonial history to moral and religious instruction, with long topographical and catalogue passages.
literary_form: Topographical and descriptive poetry with didactic and historical argument; the estate and township poem transferred to America
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets, iambic pentameter, with occasional longer stanzas
historical_context: Published in 1794 at New York, in the president's second decade, and written from the author's settled life at Greenfield Hill in Connecticut. Its models were Thomson, Goldsmith and the British descriptive school, and its subject was the newly confident Congregational township. Its political passages reflect the 1790s quarrel over French revolutionary principles and over the fate of religion in a republic.
literary_significance: It is the largest American poem of the 1790s and the standard example of the transplanted British topographical manner. Its social survey makes it a primary document for the cultural history of Connecticut. Its reputation stood high through the nineteenth century as the work of the president of Yale.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published at New York, printed by Childs and Swaine, in 1794, in one small volume; the poem is described on the title-page as being in seven parts, and later editions vary the numbering.

title: Travels in New-England and New-York
description: A survey of the country and the people of the northern states, written from journal matter and printed after the author's death. It combines topographical description, agricultural observation, statistical tables and moral and religious argument. It is the fullest early American example of the traveller's national survey.
plot_or_argument: The narrative moves through Connecticut, Massachusetts and the eastern and western parts of New York, describing towns, soils, manufactures, schools and churches as it goes. It reports conversations with farmers, clergymen and lawyers, and it argues that the prosperity of the country depends on its religious and educational institutions. Its accounts of the Dutch settlements and of the western districts give a picture of a nation in motion. The work closes with reflections on the destiny of a Christian and lettered commonwealth.
narrative_structure: Travels arranged by route and district, with journal narrative, descriptive survey, tables of numbers and inserted disquisition; posthumously edited from memoranda.
literary_form: Travel narrative and local guide; topographical and statistical survey with moral argument
historical_context: Published from the author's papers in 1821, with an enlarged four-volume issue shortly afterwards, and composed from tours taken in the last years of the eighteenth century and after the peace of 1815. Its attention to canals, schools and denominations reflects the internal-improvement moment of the era. Its author had been president of Yale since 1795.
literary_significance: It is the most systematic American portrait of the northern states before Tocqueville and a central document of the clerical survey of the republic. Its fusion of topographical detail with religious argument shows the didactic descriptive tradition continuing into the 1820s. It supplies the social map against which the native fiction of the same decade was written.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed; the volume was edited and issued after the author's death from his journals.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1821 in two volumes from the author's papers, with a four-volume edition including a memoir appearing in 1823; the earlier journey matter dates from the 1790s.

title: A Compendious Dictionary of the English Language
description: The first considerable dictionary published in the United States, a single-volume compendium intended to fix American spelling, pronunciation and usage. It gathers the common English vocabulary with the new words of the republic and adds a grammatical and orthographical preface. It is the working ancestor of the great dictionary of 1828.
plot_or_argument: The work defines the ordinary vocabulary of the language, marking parts of speech and offering usage notes rather than literary quotation. It sets out the American preferences in spelling that its author had long argued for, and it appends tables of words pronounced and spelled alike but differently written. Its front matter states the case for a national language independent of British decision. The whole is designed for the schoolroom and the counting house rather than for the scholar.
narrative_structure: Alphabetical dictionary with a doctrinal preface and appended tables; no narrative.
literary_form: Lexicography and philological writing; school and usage dictionary
historical_context: Published in 1806 after two decades of the author's spelling books and political pamphlets on language, and in the season of the American argument that a republic needed its own dictionary. Its spelling reforms answered the Federalist and nationalist claim that language is an instrument of national character. It drew on Johnson and on the technical vocabulary then entering American speech.
literary_significance: It established the authority of the American dictionary and made the lexicon a question of national policy. Its spellings passed generally into American use. It is the necessary predecessor of the 1828 work and a document of the linguistic nationalism of the early republic.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published at New Haven in 1806 in one octavo volume; it was revised and reissued through the following two decades.

title: An American Dictionary of the English Language
alternative_titles: An American Dictionary
description: The two-volume dictionary that completed the author's life work and gave American English its standard of authority. It carries a much enlarged vocabulary, definitions built from actual usage, and a preface arguing that a language grows from the people who speak it. Its spellings, its encyclopaedic entries and its moral and religious illustrations define the American reference book.
plot_or_argument: The volumes alphabetically define the whole range of ordinary, technical and scriptural words then in use in the United States, with parts of speech, etymologies and examples of application. The prefatory dissertation argues for the maturity and independence of the American language and for the authority of national usage. The appended plates and tables treat weights, measures, coins and the divisions of learning. The dictionary's entries on American institutions and words register the new republic's vocabulary as evidence.
narrative_structure: Two-volume alphabetical dictionary with prefatory dissertations on the origin, development and national character of the English language, and with appendix tables.
literary_form: Lexicography and philological writing; the national standard dictionary
historical_context: Published in 1828 after more than two decades of preparation and a tour of Europe for the study of the kindred languages, and in the year of the republic's second half-century of independence. Its claims for American linguistic independence belong to the nationalist program of the 1820s. Its scriptural and moral illustrations reflect its author's religious and political conservatism.
literary_significance: It is the foundation of American lexicography and the source of the orthographical system that American spelling still follows. Its preface is the most influential statement of the doctrine of a national language. It fixed the dictionary as an instrument of public instruction in the United States.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed; the work is lexicographical and its authority rests on its editor's long labour rather than on collective authorship.
bibliographical_notes: First published at New York in 1828 in two folio-sized quarto volumes, with a London edition arranged shortly afterwards; the American issue carries the author's name and the dedicatory and prefatory dissertations.

title: Unitarian Christianity
alternative_titles: The Baltimore Sermon
description: The sermon that gave American Unitarianism its public statement of faith and its reply to the charge of unbelief. It distinguishes the doctrinal and practical articles of the Unitarians, claims the authority of reason in religion, and refuses to make the creeds of other parties its own. Its plain, deliberate style became the manner of a movement.
plot_or_argument: The sermon first separates the doctrines on which its party is defined from the practices for which it is censured, and grants that some charges are just. It then states the Unitarian belief in one God and in the moral authority of Christ, and argues that a unitarian creed is simpler and therefore more fit for a reasonable creature. It answers the accusation that its party denies the scriptural scheme of atonement and of innate depravity. It closes by commending charity of judgment and by claiming for the conscience the duty of thinking.
narrative_structure: Occasional sermon in the discursive New England manner, divided between statement of doctrine, answer to objections and practical application.
literary_form: Homily or sermon with polemical argument; the party sermon of a religious movement
historical_context: Preached at Baltimore in May 1819, at the moment when the Unitarian controversy had divided the standing congregations of eastern Massachusetts and when the party was organizing its churches, its periodicals and its divinity school. The occasion was an ordination service, and the sermon was soon read as the public statement of a body of ministers who had not yet taken an institutional name. Its plain rhetoric was itself a claim about the relation of reason to faith in a republican country.
literary_significance: It is the founding document of American Unitarianism as a self-conscious party and one of the most influential religious statements of the early republic. Its defence of reason in religion shaped the preaching, the criticism and the social reform of the next generation. It supplies the intellectual context for the religious conscience of the literature of New England in this period.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed; the sermon was printed from the pulpit notes and reissued in the author's collected discourses.
bibliographical_notes: Published in 1819 as a separate sermon from the chapel in Federal Street, Boston, and reprinted several times within the controversy; it holds the opening place among the author's discourses.

title: The American Universal Geography
alternative_titles: The American Universal Geography; or, A View of the Present State of All the Empires, Kingdoms, States, and Republics in the Known World
description: A comprehensive geography of the world in American hands, revised and reissued for three decades and used as a school and reference book. It sets the continents, empires and trades against one another and treats the United States as the scene of a new civil and religious society. Its account of the country is bound up with the author's argument for public piety and learning.
plot_or_argument: The work describes the divisions of the earth, the states of Europe and Asia, the commerce of the world, and then passes to the American republics, their boundaries, produce, population and institutions. Statistical accounts of the states, including their inhabitants and their religious divisions, carry its argument that geography is a branch of public morality. Its later issues bring the tables and the histories of the western country up to date. It closes with the duties of a Christian nation placed among the powers of the world.
narrative_structure: Systematic geography in books and chapters, combining cosmographical description, regional accounts, statistical tables and moral and religious reflection.
literary_form: Didactic and school geography; topographical and statistical survey with religious argument
historical_context: Compiled from the author's earlier geographical work and issued in successive editions through the 1790s and after, when American schools wanted a native textbook instead of British imports. Its tables answer the first federal censuses and the post-Revolution expansion of trade. Its author was a Congregational minister and a publicist who used geography as a vehicle for the cause of religion and learning.
literary_significance: It made the systematic survey of the world available to American schools and helped to found the American trade in geographical textbooks. Its account of the republic's resources and divisions is a document of national self-description. It shows how the didactic geography carried the religious and political argument of the early republic.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed; the several editions differ greatly in extent and in the material they include.
bibliographical_notes: First published at Boston in 1793, the issue in which the title was changed; it grew out of Morse's 'The American Geography' of 1789, which was revised, enlarged and re-issued under the new name. Later editions were revised and enlarged through the early nineteenth century, and their contents differ considerably, so quotations must be tied to a named edition.

title: Annals of the American Revolution
alternative_titles: Annals of the American Revolution; or, A Record of the Causes and Events which Produced, and Terminated in the Establishment and Independence of the American Republic
description: A year-by-year record of the war of independence, compiled from documents, state papers and the published histories, and issued with a documentary apparatus. It treats the Revolution as a providential national history and arranges its matter chronologically for reference. It belongs to the wave of centennial-era preservation of founding records.
plot_or_argument: The annals follow the progress of the war from its political origins through the campaigns, the councils, the correspondence and the treaties, entering each year's principal events in order. They interweave the operations in the northern and southern states and at sea, and record the civil measures of the states and of Congress. Documents and letters are printed at length or abstracted, with notes identifying their sources. The work ends with the peace and with the establishment of the government it treats as the fruit of the contest.
narrative_structure: Chronological annals with entries arranged by year and campaign, supported by printed documents and editorial notes.
literary_form: History and chronicle with documentary editing; the national annalistic record
historical_context: Published at Hartford in 1824, in the decade of the fiftieth-anniversary celebrations, the tours of Lafayette and the first great editorial enterprises for the founding records. Its compiler was a Congregational minister and geographer who read the Revolution as a religious as well as a political event. The book anticipates the documentary series edited by the historical societies of the following decade.
literary_significance: It is an early American attempt to fix the chronology of the Revolution from sources rather than from memory, and it stands beside the editorial work of the same generation. Its providential reading of national history was characteristic of the clerical nationalism of New England. It supplies a reference frame for the historical fiction of the 1820s.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed; the volume also contains edited documentary papers relating to the war.
bibliographical_notes: First published at Hartford in 1824; the title-page carries the long explanatory subtitle reproduced in this record's alternative titles.

title: The Diplomatic Correspondence of the American Revolution
description: A twelve-volume editorial collection of the letters, instructions and negotiations of the American ministers abroad during the war of independence, printed from the state papers and furnished with biographical and historical notes. It was the first great documentary edition of the founding period and made the diplomacy of the Revolution readable as history. Its editorial method set the standard for the American historical enterprise.
plot_or_argument: The volumes gather the correspondence of the commissioners in France and Spain, the negotiations for the treaties of amity and commerce, the instructions of Congress and the reports of the envoys in the northern courts. Each document is placed in chronological order and accompanied by notes identifying persons, explaining transactions and citing the parallel records. The editor supplies biographical memoirs and historical dissertations that turn the papers into a narrative of the foreign struggle for recognition. The collection closes with the peace and its immediate diplomatic consequences.
narrative_structure: Multi-volume documentary edition arranged chronologically by correspondent and year, with editorial notes, memoirs and dissertations interposed.
literary_form: Editorial collection of state papers with commentary; documentary history and letters
historical_context: Published at Boston from 1829, with the closing volumes in 1830, in the season of the new American historical societies and of public interest in the founding records. Its editor had just taken charge of a national periodical and was assembling the materials for the biographical works that made him the chief American editor of his generation. The edition answered the British possession of much of the diplomatic record.
literary_significance: It founded the scholarly documentary edition in America and created the archival basis on which later histories of the Revolution were written. Its editorial apparatus established the American model of the annotated national papers. It is the touchstone of the era's claim that the republic could preserve and interpret its own records.
attribution_notes: The collection is an editorial compilation of documents written by many hands; the record is assigned in the batch map to the editor who chose, arranged and annotated it.
bibliographical_notes: Published at Boston in twelve volumes from 1829 to 1830, issued by the firms named on the volumes and printed for the editor; a related later compilation revised and enlarged this series.

title: The Buccaneer, and Other Poems
alternative_titles: The Buccaneer
description: The first collected volume of the Boston and Cambridge poet who was also the most discerning critic of his generation in America. Its title poem is a narrative of the sea in the romantic manner, and the accompanying pieces treat passion, solitude and the power of scenery. The book introduced to American readers the command of blank verse associated with the review circle of the United States.
plot_or_argument: The title poem tells of a buoyant and lawless sea-rover whose career of plunder ends in remorse and in a death that the ocean itself seems to witness. Its narrative is interrupted by invocations to the sea, to the storm and to the memory of the beloved. The shorter poems pass from love and loss to meditative observation of New England and Italian scenery. The volume's dominant movement is from romantic action to the moral seriousness that its author later brought to criticism.
narrative_structure: Collected volume with one dominant metrical tale of the sea, followed by lyrics and meditative pieces of occasional origin.
principal_characters: The buccaneer; the beloved of the meditative pieces
literary_form: Metrical tale and romance in verse, with lyric and meditative poems; the maritime branch of the American romantic poem
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse for the metrical tale, with iambic lyric stanzas for the shorter poems
historical_context: Published in 1827, when its author was an editor and critic in Boston and Cambridge and a member of the circle that shaped the American review. Its subject belongs to the New England commerce with the sea and to the Byron-derived romance of the outlaw. The volume's reception was bound up with the quarrels of the native periodicals over the possibility of an American poetry.
literary_significance: It is one of the ablest American metrical tales of the 1820s and a landmark of the maritime strand in American romantic verse. Its author's criticism made the volume a document of the transatlantic argument about poetry. It supplies the link between the review culture of Boston and the native romance of the sea.
attribution_notes: Attribution undisputed; a small number of handbook accounts date the first collection to the late 1820s, and the year here follows the literary histories consulted.
bibliographical_notes: First collected in 1827; a volume of Poems and Prose Writings gathering the same matter was issued in the following decade, and the earlier periodical appearance of the title poem is generally assumed but is not dated in this record.
